newsitem.title: USA: Heavy snow blankets Kansas, more moisture expected.
newsitem.headline: Heavy snow blankets Kansas, more moisture expected.

text.p: Heavy snow fell across western Kansas and eastern Colorado early Monday, bringing much-needed moisture to winter wheat fields and forecasts called for another chance of precipitation late Tuesday, meteorologists said.

"Colby, Kansas, was the winner with a foot of snow," said Joel Burgio, meteorologist with Weather Services Corp. "That melted down to about 0.25 to 0.4 inch of precipitation. That's very good moisture for this time of year in that region."
Snow was tapering off by mid-morning.
Temperatures were expected to fall to the single digits Fahrenheit across northern Kansas early Tuesday.
Weather Express forecaster Fred Gesser said Monday's snow storm hit dry patches of western Kansas and southwest portions could see some more moisture with Tuesday's storm.
Some farmers have been concerned with dry weather and there were reports last month of blowing topsoil as strong winds swept across parched fields.
Another system was expected to bring rain and snow to western Texas and the Oklahoma Panhandle late Tuesday and into Wednesday with up to six inches of snow possible, he said.
"What we have in the future is a storm system evolving today and tomorrow," Gesser said.
The next storm system was expected to push north and east this week, bringing a chance for more precipitation in the water-logged regions of central Illinois, Gesser said.
Rising water fed by heavy rains last Thursday and Friday has snagged barge traffic on the Illinois River and forced the closure of several locks, a U.S. Army Corp of Engineers official said.
Additional precipitation could further disrupt movement.
Gesser said the moisture would likely fall in the form of snow but forecasts for warmer weather later this week suggested the snow would melt quickly.
That could cause more run-off problems on the Illinois River.
"It looks like for the most part it will be snow but it will be wet snow," Gesser said. "It's going to melt in a hurry."
Weather Services Corp's Burgio said long-range forecasts indicated another storm system could hit central Illinois on Saturday, bringing more rain.
